claims.text: The as-cast alloy has a coarser grain structure than a suitably thermomechanically processed alloy.
The as-cast alloy has undergone minimal grain-boundary engineering.
Hot rolling can refine grain size and eliminate defects in as-cast alloys.
Rapid annealing can promote recrystallization while limiting grain coarsening and thereby reduce grain size.
The proposed combination of hot rolling and rapid annealing will produce an ultrafine-grained Ti65(AlCrNbV)28Zr-based alloy.
An optimized post-annealing step will relieve residual stresses while retaining the ultrafine-grained structure.
Grain refinement increases yield strength by making grain boundaries barriers to dislocation motion through the Hall–Petch effect.
A high density of grain boundaries provides abundant nucleation sites for a continuous protective oxide scale.
The continuous oxide scale generated by grain refinement reduces the alloy's high-temperature oxidation rate.
The grain-boundary-mediated protective-scale mechanism also improves corrosion resistance in 3.5 wt.% NaCl.
Optimized thermomechanical processing will give the treated alloy higher yield strength than the as-cast alloy.
Optimized thermomechanical processing will reduce oxidation mass gain at 800 °C relative to the as-cast alloy.
Optimized thermomechanical processing will reduce corrosion current density relative to the as-cast alloy.
The as-cast baseline has higher oxidation rates than the processed alloy.
The as-cast baseline has higher corrosion rates than the processed alloy.
Excessive residual stress can accelerate grain-boundary oxidation and eliminate the environmental-resistance benefit.
Over-refinement can accelerate grain-boundary diffusion and diminish protective oxide behavior.
Grain coarsening during service can cause accelerated grain-boundary diffusion and loss of protective oxide behavior.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis associates accelerated grain-boundary diffusion with over-refinement and therefore high grain-boundary density, whereas the boundary field also attributes accelerated grain-boundary diffusion to grain coarsening, which reduces grain-boundary density. The latter link is not reconciled with the stated mechanism.
